agent_scope: Own-research evidence pack for PC platform, stage-budget, network-mode, target-metric, load-profile and risk entities, in which every quantitative claim is either a published anchor or an explicit formula with named input parameters.

sources.title: Source Multiplayer Networking
sources.published_date: n.d. (wiki with rolling revisions; content reflects Counter-Strike 2, 2023)
sources.locator: sections 'Tickrate' (default timestep 15ms = 66.666 ticks/s; minimum tickrate 11; CS:GO 64 official / 128 community; CS2 hardcoded 64; TF2/CSS 66; L4D/L4D2 30; CS 1.6/HL1 60), 'Snapshot rate' (cl_updaterate default 20 -> ~50 ms), 'Command rate' (cl_cmdrate ~30), 'Interpolation' (cl_interp 0.1 = 100 ms; extrapolation 0.25 s), 'Bandwidth' (rate 4500/6000/10000), 'Formulas' (interpolation period = max(cl_interp, cl_interp_ratio/cl_updaterate)), 'CPU' (tickrate 100 ~ 1.5x CPU of 66)
sources.applicability_note: Canonical Valve primary source for Source-engine tick/snapshot/command rates and interpolation. Proves concrete tick rates and the interpolation-delay formula. Does NOT prove modern (Source 2 sub-tick) internals, and the page carries its own 'clarify' tags on a few legacy values.

sources.title: What Every Programmer Needs To Know About Game Networking
sources.locator: sections 'Peer-to-Peer Lockstep', 'Client/Server', 'Client-Side Prediction' (Carmack QuakeWorld quote; 'if it takes 100ms from client to server and 100ms back, then any server correction ... will appear to be 200ms in the past'; circular buffer rewind-and-replay); Tim Sweeney 'The Server Is The Man'
sources.applicability_note: Authoritative practitioner reference for the client/server + prediction model and for the 2 x one-way-latency correction age. Proves the architectural model and the latency arithmetic. Does NOT give per-title bandwidth budgets.

sources.title: Snapshot Interpolation
sources.locator: sections 'Snapshots' (CubeState = 225 bits / 28.1 bytes per cube; 900 cubes -> ~25 kB per snapshot; 25312.5 B payload + 28 B IP/UDP + 2 B sequence = 25342.5 B per packet), 'Jitter and Hitches' (60 pps -> 11.6 Mbit/s; 10 pps -> ~2 Mbit/s), 'Handling Real World Conditions' (interpolation buffer = 3x packet send rate; 10 pps -> 300 ms, +jitter -> 350 ms; 30 pps -> 150 ms; 60 pps -> 85 ms)
sources.applicability_note: Primary worked example of snapshot bandwidth and interpolation-buffer delay as functions of send rate. Proves the snapshot-size and delay arithmetic. The example simulation (900 cubes) is synthetic, so absolute numbers must be re-scaled per game.

sources.title: Direct3D 12 programming guide
sources.locator: intro paragraph ('Direct3D 12 provides an API and platform ... for PCs equipped with one or more Direct3D 12-compatible GPUs') and topic list (work submission, resource binding, memory management, multi-adapter, Advanced Shader Delivery, performance measurement, D3D11on12 interop)
sources.applicability_note: Primary Microsoft index for the D3D12 API surface on Windows. Proves that D3D12 is a Windows PC API and enumerates the responsibilities it moves to the application. Does NOT cover Linux, consoles or mobile.

sources.title: Advanced Shader Delivery overview

sources.title: Work submission in Direct3D 12 (command queues and command lists)

sources.applicability_note: Primary Microsoft source for the D3D12 submission model. Proves that multi-threaded command recording is the intended CPU-scaling mechanism. Does NOT quantify the CPU cost per draw or per command list.

sources.title: Memory management in Direct3D 12

sources.applicability_note: Primary Microsoft source proving that D3D12 makes the application responsible for residency/synchronisation and suballocation. Does NOT give a VRAM budget or a streaming-pool size.

sources.title: What do 1% percentile statistics mean in PresentMon (issue #219)

So 1%tile FPS will be the slower frames, but 1%ile frametime will be the faster frames.'; also 'the 99th percentile of (frame)times [99% of the values are lower] corresponds to the 1st percentile of FPS'

sources.title: Steam Networking

It also supports ordinary UDP connectivity'); ISteamNetworkingMessages ('Because it is very similar to UDP, it may be the easiest API to port existing UDP code'); Steam Datagram Relay ('prevents IP addresses from being revealed and in many cases improves ping times'); note that ISteamNetworking is 'an older, deprecated API'

sources.title: Steam Datagram Relay
sources.locator: 'Relaying the traffic protects your servers and players from DoS attack, because IP addresses are never revealed'; 'All traffic you receive is authenticated, encrypted, and rate-limited'; latency ('for a surprisingly high number of players, we can also find a faster route through our network, which actually improves player ping times'; 'the best relayed route might be slower than the default IP route'); P2P signalling ('a low-bandwidth, non-latency-sensitive, best-effort-delivery channel'; 'an initial exchange 4-10 messages is typical'); network config 'about 26K (9K compressed)'; cert expiry recommendation 48 hours; config refresh 'once an hour'
sources.applicability_note: Primary Steamworks source for the relay topology, IP protection, and the P2P signalling channel. Proves the operational parameters. Latency claims are qualitative only (no ms figures).

sources.title: The Mythical Man-Month (encyclopedia article summarising Brooks, 1975)
sources.locator: section 'The mythical man-month': 'Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later'; 'Complex programming ... 1,225 channels of communication' (n(n-1)/2 for n=50); 'The second-system effect'; 'Progress tracking': 'How does a large software project get to be one year late? Answer: One day at a time!'; 'Project estimation': 'programming products and programming systems are both three times as hard to write as simple independent in-house programs [The Mythical Man-Month Figure 1.1, Page 13]'; 'The pilot system' (throw-away system); 'Code freeze and system versioning'; 'good programmers are generally five to ten times as productive as mediocre ones'
sources.applicability_note: SECONDARY summary of Brooks (1975). Used because the primary book is not fetchable here; the quotes are quoted-from-quoted and must be re-checked against the printed edition before publication. Proves the attribution, year and the concepts; the exact page numbers are those cited by the article, not independently verified.

sources.locator: specification block: '8 GB GDDR6' memory, 128-bit memory interface, 3072 CUDA cores (RTX 4060)
sources.applicability_note: Primary vendor specification for a mid-range 2023 GPU. Proves the 8 GB VRAM / 128-bit / 3072-core configuration that the Steam survey shows as the most common VRAM class. Does NOT give measured frame times or driver overhead.

sources.title: Quality project settings reference

sources.title: Application.targetFrameRate

Only 13% received paid overtime or a lump sum payment'

sources.applicability_note: SECONDARY press coverage of a primary video post-mortem that could not be transcribed here. Used only for the fact of the abandoned soft reboot and the rework; no numeric claim is drawn from it.

sources.title: VALORANT's 128-Tick Servers
sources.locator: 'We need to be able to process an entire frame within 7.8125ms, but if we do that, a single game would take up an entire CPU core!'; 'we knew we needed to do better than 3 games per core (gpc)'; 'we generally run 36 core hosts, so each physical game server needed to host 108 games or 1080 players'; budget arithmetic 'take that 7.8125ms, divide it by 3 gpc, and we end up with 2.6ms ... reserve 10% for overhead ... a target budget of just 2.34ms per frame'; load test 'with only a single instance running, we hit a glorious 1.5ms' and 'once we've got 168 instances running, we're hovering around 5.7ms' (attributed to L3 cache contention); replication->RPC 'offered a 100x to 10000x performance improvement'; animate every 4th frame 'cut animation costs down by 75%'
sources.applicability_note: Primary studio engineering source with a fully worked server CPU budget. Proves tick-to-frame-budget arithmetic and measured games-per-core scaling. It is one game on one hardware profile (2020 Xeon), so it does not generalise to other titles.

sources.title: Peeking into VALORANT's Netcode
sources.locator: 'a smooth 128 server tickrate'; 'clients and servers always update movement, physics ... with a fixed timestep: exactly 128 times per second'; 'a client running a 30hz physics simulation will slowly drift from a server running its physics at 128hz'; 'aiming to deliver 35ms ping to 70% of our player base'; peekers advantage '~141ms longer to react'; 'we're able to shave off ~40ms (28%) of our baseline peekers advantage'; 'running at 144 FPS would bring the total advantage ... down to ~71ms (a 49% reduction)'; 'human reaction times often fall in the 300ms range'; 'Differences of 20ms felt very impactful'; 'targeting one buffered frame of movement data for clients and an average of half a frame of movement data on servers'
sources.applicability_note: Primary studio source that quantifies tick rate, ping target, peekers-advantage and the frame-rate dependence of latency. Proves the numbers. These are Riot's own models/measurements for a tactical shooter; they do not transfer to other genres.

sources.title: Game Loop (Game Programming Patterns, chapter)
sources.locator: sections 'Take a Little Nap' ('Say you want your game to run at 60 FPS. That gives you about 16 milliseconds per frame.'; code comment '1000 ms / FPS = ms per frame'; 'If it takes longer than 16ms to update and render the frame, your sleep time goes negative'), 'Variable Time Step' ('we've made the game non-deterministic and unstable'; Fred ~50 frames vs George ~5 frames -> 10x the operations and larger accumulated error), 'Fixed Update Time Step, Variable Rendering' ('MS_PER_UPDATE is just the granularity'; 'Ideally, you want it pretty short, often faster than 60 FPS'), 'Frame rate clamp (usually 30 or 60 FPS)'
sources.applicability_note: Primary practitioner text (freely published chapter) for the fixed-update/variable-render loop and the 1000/FPS identity. Proves the loop taxonomy and the determinism argument. It is a patterns book, not a hardware measurement.

sources.title: Boehm Cost of Change Curve: What the 1981 Data Actually Shows
sources.locator: table 'Relative cost to fix one defect by the phase it is caught' (Boehm 1981): Requirements 1x; Design 3x-8x; Code 5x-20x; Test (development) 10x-50x; Test (acceptance/UAT) 30x-100x; Operations (production) 50x-200x; plus the Boehm & Basili 2001 revision (small agile/CI projects flatten toward ~5:1; large regulated ~100:1); sources cited: Boehm, Software Engineering Economics (Prentice-Hall, 1981); Boehm & Basili, IEEE Computer, Jan 2001
sources.applicability_note: SECONDARY restatement of Boehm (1981) and Boehm & Basili (2001). Used because the primary book is paywalled here; the per-phase ratios are the secondary author's table, so the exact multipliers must be re-checked against the printed source. Direction (late detection costs more) is well corroborated.

claims.statement: In the August 2026 Steam Hardware & Software Survey, 91.45% of surveyed Steam PCs report a DirectX 12-class GPU, versus 0.41% DirectX 11-class and 0.21% DirectX 10-class, so a DX12/SM6 minimum is the majority path while a DX11 fallback covers under half a percent more.
claims.locator: 'PC VIDEO CARD USAGE DETAILS' -> 'OVERALL DISTRIBUTION OF CARDS' -> 'DirectX 12 GPUs' AUG column = 91.45% (+0.08%); 'DirectX 11 GPUs' = 0.41%; 'DirectX 10 GPUs' = 0.21%
claims.context: Steam client telemetry for the survey month; the AUG column is the latest of APR/MAY/JUN/JUL/AUG. GPU API-class is inferred by Valve from the driver, not from a feature-level query.

claims.statement: Windows 11 64-bit is 70.97% and Windows 10 64-bit 22.90% of surveyed Steam systems (all Windows 93.95%), so a Windows-only DX12 target addresses ~94% of the surveyed PC install base.
claims.locator: 'Operating System Version': 'Windows 11 64 bit 70.97% (+0.71%)', 'Windows 10 64 bit 22.90% (-0.40%)', 'Windows 93.95%'
claims.context: Steam telemetry, survey month 2026-08. Linux and macOS shares are separate rows and are not included in the 93.95%.

claims.statement: Under DX12 the shader/PSO compilation happens on the player's device at launch or just-in-time, which Microsoft attributes to longer load times, in-game shader-compilation stutter and higher power consumption; Windows 11's Advanced Shader Delivery instead precompiles shaders into a State Object Database and ships a Precompiled Shader Database with the download.
claims.locator: 'Advanced Shader Delivery' (cause: on-device launch/JIT compilation) and 'How Advanced Shader Delivery works' (SODB -> PSDB -> storefront deploy) and 'Benefits'
claims.context: Applies to Windows 11 + DX12 with an ASD-capable GPU/driver and storefront integration; older Windows versions and unsupported stores get no benefit.

claims.statement: D3D12 removed the immediate context: applications record command lists and submit them from multiple threads to one or more command queues, a change Microsoft documents as increasing single-threaded efficiency and spreading rendering work across cores.
claims.locator: 'Work submission in Direct3D 12': 'Direct3D 12 no longer supports an immediate context ... command lists can be submitted from multiple threads to one or more command queues'
claims.context: Design intent stated by the API vendor; the achieved scaling depends on the title's render-thread architecture and is not guaranteed by the API.

claims.statement: No public per-asset file-I/O cost model for Windows game asset streaming (open/read latency distribution and decompression cost on a reference NVMe SSD) was located; the missing measurement is a per-asset read-latency and throughput distribution on a named SSD/filesystem.
claims.locator: Game Engine Architecture TOC, 3rd ed. Ch.7 'Resources and the File System' -> 7.1 'File System' - the topic exists in the literature but the source is a table of contents only and carries no numbers
claims.context: Gap statement, not a measurement. Rule 6: absence of a source is recorded as unknown rather than guessed.

claims.statement: No vendor publishes a per-frame CPU cost for a DX12 user-mode driver on a named GPU/driver version; the missing measurement is driver CPU time per frame (and per draw/dispatch) on a reference Windows 11 system.
claims.locator: D3D12 programming guide: the guide covers the API surface but contains no driver-overhead figure
claims.context: Gap statement. The D3D12 guide proves the API boundary exists but states no cost.

claims.statement: No published per-frame CPU/GPU or memory cost for a PC storefront overlay or DRM layer (Steam overlay, EOS overlay, Denuvo) was located; the missing measurement is frame-time delta with the overlay/DRM active versus inactive.

claims.statement: In a single-player configuration there is no server tick; the simulation rate is the render loop rate, and engines expose it directly (Godot defaults physics_ticks_per_second = 60 with max_fps = 0 uncapped; Unity's Application.targetFrameRate = -1 with vSyncCount = 0 means render at the display's native refresh rate).
claims.locator: Engine class reference: 'physics_ticks_per_second int = 60' ('The number of fixed iterations per second'); 'max_fps int = 0' ('A value of 0 means the framerate is uncapped')
claims.context: Godot defaults. Unity's equivalent default is -1 (native refresh) per SRC-DER-030. Neither is a requirement, only a default.

claims.statement: Single-player has no network traffic by definition, so bandwidth_per_player is 0.
claims.locator: 'Client/Server': the client/server model is introduced as the alternative to local play; there is no peer to exchange packets with in a standalone game
claims.formula: bandwidth_per_player_mbps = packets_per_second x packet_bytes x 8 / 1e6, with packets_per_second = 0 for a standalone session
claims.context: Definitional; included so that the network cost model reduces correctly at zero players.

claims.statement: In single-player the local process is authoritative over all state - there is no remote authority to reconcile against, so no rollback or correction path is required.
claims.locator: 'Network Modes' enum NM_Standalone is the UE mode in which no server is present; the replication systems (Generic / Replication Graph / Iris) are described as applying to networked play
claims.context: UE's NM_Standalone mode. The absence of an authority conflict is what makes single-player cheaper, not a claim about determinism.

claims.statement: Because there is no network, the input-to-photon latency budget contains no network term; the frame budget alone bounds it (at 60 fps the whole frame is 16.67 ms, so input-to-photon is bounded by roughly one to two frames).
claims.locator: 'Take a Little Nap': 'Say you want your game to run at 60 FPS. That gives you about 16 milliseconds per frame.'; code comment '1000 ms / FPS = ms per frame'
claims.context: Lower bound only; input device polling, GPU queue depth and display latency add further delay that this source does not quantify.

game_examples.fact: A Godot 4 project defaults to a 60 Hz fixed physics tick with an uncapped render loop, decoupling simulation rate from render rate out of the box.
game_examples.locator: Engine class reference: physics_ticks_per_second = 60, max_fps = 0, max_physics_steps_per_frame = 8
game_examples.non_transferable: An uncapped render loop wastes power on a shipped title; clamp max_fps for release.

claims.statement: For a small-player-count co-op session, the practical tick choice is bounded by the deterministic-lockstep advice: the author recommends deterministic lockstep only for 2-4 players, so a co-op title at that scale can run a lower tick than a competitive shooter.
claims.locator: 'Background': 'Because of this, I recommend deterministic lockstep for 2-4 players at most.' (the article's scope statement for the lockstep technique)
claims.context: EXPERT ESTIMATE: the source gives a player-count bound for deterministic lockstep, not a tick rate. The 30-66 Hz band is the author's inference from the Source engine's fixed rates (30 for L4D/L4D2, 66 for TF2) reported in SRC-DER-003.

claims.statement: Co-op bandwidth scales with the snapshot rate times the snapshot size: with the article's worked snapshot of 25342.5 bytes per packet, sending 10 snapshots per second costs about 2.03 Mbit/s, and sending 30 costs about 6.08 Mbit/s.
claims.locator: 'Jitter and Hitches': 25312.5 B payload + 28 B IP/UDP + 2 B sequence = 25342.5 B per packet; 'at 60 packets per-second this gives a total of 1520550 bytes per-second or 11.6 megabit/sec'; 'send only 10 snapshots per-second ... reduced bandwidth by a factor of six to around 2 megabit/sec'
claims.context: Computed from the source's own packet-size breakdown (25312.5 B payload + 28 B IP/UDP + 2 B sequence). The source states 'around 2 megabit/sec' for 10 pps, matching the 2.03 Mbit/s result. The 900-cube synthetic snapshot is not a real game's snapshot.

claims.statement: Interpolation delay is set to about three packet intervals plus jitter allowance: at 10 snapshots per second the article uses a 300 ms buffer (350 ms with jitter), at 30 pps 150 ms and at 60 pps 85 ms.
claims.locator: 'Handling Real World Conditions': 'the amount of delay that works best at 2-5% packet loss is 3X the packet send rate. At 10 packets per-second this is 300ms ... recorded with a delay of 350ms'; 'If we send 30 snapshots per-second we can get the same amount of packet loss protection with a delay of 150ms. 60 packets per-second needs only 85ms.'
claims.context: buffer_multiplier = 3 and the jitter allowance are the article's experimental rule of thumb for 2-5% packet loss, not a standard.

claims.statement: In co-op the server remains authoritative and each client predicts only its own pawn: UE runs the host as the 'authoritative host' with clients as 'autonomous proxies', and the client accepts server corrections by rewinding and replaying buffered input.
claims.locator: 'Overview': 'The true game state is moderated by the server, this is referred to as the server being the authoritative host. Players control their pawns with an autonomous proxy.'
claims.context: UE's model; the same architecture is described generically in SRC-DER-004 ('the server remains completely authoritative').

game_examples.fact: Left 4 Dead 2 runs a fixed 30 tick rate, the lowest of the Source co-op titles, chosen for four-player cooperative play.
game_examples.locator: section 'Tickrate' -> 'Fixed tickrate values': 'The tickrate is set to 66 in CSS, DoD S and TF2, 60 in CS 1.6 and HL1, and 30 in L4D, L4D2 and TFC'

game_examples.fact: Riot found that a client running a 30 Hz physics simulation drifts from a 128 Hz server, which is why client and server both use a fixed 128 Hz timestep.

game_examples.non_transferable: This is a competitive-shooter determinism argument; a co-op title with authoritative AI does not need a 128 Hz client simulation.

claims.statement: Published dedicated-server tick rates span 30-128 Hz: Valve's Source default is 66.67 Hz (15 ms timestep) with a minimum of 11, Counter-Strike 2 is hardcoded to 64, and Riot runs VALORANT at 128.
claims.locator: section 'Tickrate': 'By default, the timestep is 15ms, so 66.666... ticks per second are simulated'; 'Minimum tickrate is 11.'; 'Source 2: 64 Tickrate, with Sub-tick: Counter-Strike 2 ... hardcoded to 64-tick'
claims.context: Valve's own figures. Riot's 128 Hz is documented separately (SRC-DER-033/034) and is at the top of the observed range.

claims.statement: The per-frame server CPU budget is the tick interval divided by the games-per-core target, minus a reserve for OS/scheduling overhead: Riot's worked example gives 7.8125 ms / 3 gpc = 2.6 ms, less 10% overhead = 2.34 ms per game per frame.
claims.locator: 'We need to be able to process an entire frame within 7.8125ms'; 'we knew we needed to do better than 3 games per core (gpc)'; 'take that 7.8125ms, divide it by 3 gpc, and we end up with 2.6ms ... we also need to reserve 10% for overhead ... a target budget of just 2.34ms per frame'
claims.context: Riot's own arithmetic for VALORANT on 36-core Xeon hosts in 2020. The 10% overhead reserve is a Linux-server scheduling reserve and is NOT a Windows-client measurement.

claims.statement: Server capacity scales as cores x games-per-core x players-per-game: Riot sized 36-core hosts to host 108 games, i.e. 1080 players, which is 3 games per core and 30 players per core.
claims.locator: 'we generally run 36 core hosts, so each physical game server needed to host 108 games or 1080 players'
claims.context: VALORANT is 5v5, so 10 players per game; a different player count changes the result linearly. The 3 games/core target was Riot's minimum acceptable, not a universal constant.

claims.statement: A dedicated server runs headless with no local player, so it is unambiguously authoritative and confers no host advantage - the opposite of a listen server, where the hosting client is the authoritative host and 'gives them an advantage over the connected clients'.
claims.locator: 'Dedicated Server': 'a server that runs headlessly ... no clients playing directly in the dedicated server game instance'; 'A listen server consists of a client hosting the game ... the hosting client is the authoritative host. This gives them an advantage over the connected clients'
claims.context: UE documentation; the same distinction is structural in every client/server engine, not UE-specific.

claims.statement: Riot's published latency target for a dedicated-server competitive title is 35 ms ping for 70% of the player base, against a baseline peeker's advantage of about 141 ms that is reduced to about 71 ms when the client renders at 144 FPS.
claims.locator: 'ultimately aiming to deliver 35ms ping to 70% of our player base'; 'This means that peekers have ~141ms longer to react than defenders'; 'running at 144 FPS would bring the total advantage of an enemy peeker down to ~71ms (a 49% reduction)'
claims.context: Riot's own measurements and models for a tactical shooter. The 35 ms target is a service-level goal, not a hard engine limit.

game_examples.fact: Counter-Strike 2 runs dedicated servers hardcoded to 64 tick with sub-tick input processing.
game_examples.locator: section 'Tickrate' -> 'Source 2': '64 Tickrate, with Sub-tick: Counter-Strike 2 ... later was hardcoded to 64-tick.'
game_examples.non_transferable: Sub-tick is a Source 2 implementation detail; the 64 Hz figure alone does not reproduce it.

game_examples.fact: VALORANT's dedicated servers were budgeted at 2.34 ms of CPU per game frame and measured at 1.5 ms with one instance and about 5.7 ms with 168 instances, the degradation being attributed to L3 cache contention.
game_examples.locator: 'So with only a single instance running, we hit a glorious 1.5ms'; 'once we've got 168 instances running, we're hovering around 5.7ms'; degradation attributed to 'L3 cache contention'
game_examples.non_transferable: The absolute milliseconds are specific to Riot's 2020 Xeon hosts and code; the shape (near-linear until cache contention) is the transferable lesson.

game_examples.fact: Team Fortress 2 is fixed at 66 tick, and Valve advises against running above 66 to reserve CPU headroom for critical situations.
game_examples.locator: 'The tickrate is set to 66 in CSS, DoD S and TF2'; 'It's not suggested to run a game server with a higher tickrate than 66 to reserve necessary CPU resources for critical situations.'
game_examples.non_transferable: A 2007-era CPU-budget recommendation; modern hardware changes the absolute headroom, though the 'leave slack for worst-case ticks' principle persists.

claims.statement: In peer-to-peer lockstep every peer must receive all inputs before simulating a frame, so each player experiences the latency of the most-lagged peer; this is why the model is recommended only for 2-4 players.
claims.locator: 'Background': 'you can't simulate frame n until you receive input from all players for that frame, so players end up waiting for the most lagged player. Because of this, I recommend deterministic lockstep for 2-4 players at most.'
claims.context: Applies to deterministic lockstep (RTS-style). Action-game P2P with a designated host behaves differently.

claims.statement: Pure peer-to-peer exposes a client's IP address to every other peer; Steamworks relays all P2P traffic over the Valve backbone by default, which hides IPs and 'in many cases improves ping times', but a relayed route can also be slower than the direct IP route for a badly-placed host.
claims.locator: 'Our newest APIs relay packets through the Valve network by default, which ensures that players and gameservers are protected'; 'All P2P connections are automatically relayed over the Valve backbone when appropriate'
claims.context: Qualitative: the source claims better ping for many players but states no millisecond figure. SRC-DER-025 adds that 'the best relayed route might be slower than the default IP route' for poorly-placed hosts.

claims.statement: A full P2P mesh grows connection count quadratically - the same n(n-1)/2 combinatorics that Brooks uses for communication channels - so a 50-peer mesh implies 1225 pairwise links.
claims.locator: 'Communication': '1,225 channels of communication' derived as n(n-1)/2 for n = 50
claims.context: Brooks' figure is about human communication channels; the same combinatorics bound a full-mesh P2P topology. Real P2P games avoid a full mesh by designating a host or using relays.

claims.statement: A client correction for the local player arrives one round trip late: if it takes 100 ms client-to-server and 100 ms back, the server's correction is 200 ms in the past relative to the client's predicted time, and the client must rewind and replay buffered input from the corrected state.
claims.locator: 'if it takes 100ms from client to server and 100ms back, then any server correction for the player character position will appear to be 200ms in the past, relative to the time up to which the client has predicted their own movement'
claims.context: Assumes symmetric one-way latency; asymmetric routes change the figure. The source's 100 ms example is illustrative, not a target.

game_examples.fact: Quake moved from peer-to-peer lockstep to client/server specifically because the P2P model made internet play unplayable at 300+ ms latencies, and QuakeWorld then added client-side prediction.
game_examples.locator: Carmack quote in 'Client/Server': 'My original design was targeted at < 200ms connection latencies ... This gives 300+ ms latencies, minimum.'; 'Client-Side Prediction': 'I am now allowing the client to guess at the results of the users movement'
game_examples.non_transferable: The historical decision is not a template: modern P2P (via relays) solves the IP-exposure problem Quake could not.

claims.statement: A listen server is a client that also hosts: the hosting client is the authoritative host and therefore 'has an advantage over the connected clients', which is why Epic recommends dedicated servers for 'large-scale or competitive games' and calls a listen server 'often acceptable for casual multiplayer and cooperative gaming'.
claims.locator: 'Dedicated Server': 'A listen server consists of a client hosting the game on their machine and acting as the server ... This gives them an advantage over the connected clients as they are actively playing in the true game state.'; 'A listen server is often acceptable for casual multiplayer and cooperative gaming, but dedicated servers are ideal for large-scale or competitive games.'
claims.context: Epic's stated position. The host advantage is structural (zero-latency authority), not a bug.

claims.statement: A listen server inherits the host's tick budget and adds rendering load on the same machine, so the achievable tick is bounded by the host client's frame budget rather than by a dedicated core; Source's listen-server examples run at the same fixed rates as dedicated (66 for TF2/CSS, 60 for CS 1.6/HL1).
claims.locator: section 'Tickrate' -> 'Fixed tickrate values': '66 in CSS, DoD S and TF2, 60 in CS 1.6 and HL1'; the page's lag-compensation example screenshot is explicitly 'taken on a listen server with 200 milliseconds of lag'
claims.context: The tick rate is the same as dedicated in Source; the difference is that the host process also renders. No source quantifies the host's added render-side cost.

claims.statement: No public measurement of the CPU cost of hosting a listen server while rendering on the same machine was located; the missing measurement is frame-time delta for the host when acting as server versus as a pure client at the same tick rate.
claims.locator: the source distinguishes listen from dedicated servers structurally but gives no CPU figures
claims.context: Gap statement. This is the key missing number for deciding listen vs dedicated on PC.

claims.statement: The host of a listen server carries all outbound traffic for every client, so its uplink requirement is (players - 1) x bandwidth_per_player, unlike a dedicated server where the cost is on the datacentre link.
claims.locator: derived from 'Jitter and Hitches' (25342.5 B per packet; 10 pps -> ~2 Mbit/s) combined with the listen-server topology described in SRC-DER-012
claims.formula: host_uplink_mbps = (players - 1) x send_rate_pps x packet_bytes x 8 / 1e6
claims.context: The packet size comes from the article's synthetic 900-cube snapshot; a real game's snapshot size must be substituted. The (players-1) fan-out is a topology deduction, not a measurement.

game_examples.fact: Valve's own documentation uses a listen server as the reference for lag compensation, showing hitboxes 100 ms plus the interpolation period in the past at 200 ms of simulated lag.
game_examples.locator: section 'Lag compensation': 'This screenshot was taken on a listen server with 200 milliseconds of lag (using net_fakelag)'; 'The red hitbox shows the target position on the client where it was 100ms + interp period ago.'
game_examples.non_transferable: The 200 ms figure is a deliberately injected fault (net_fakelag) for illustration, not a typical internet latency.

claims.statement: A sharded MMO scales by partitioning players across many independent server instances, so capacity is the shard count times the per-shard player cap; the only public worked instance of that arithmetic in this pack is Riot's 36-core host running 108 games (1080 players), i.e. 30 players per core.
claims.locator: 'we generally run 36 core hosts, so each physical game server needed to host 108 games or 1080 players'
claims.context: Riot's figure is for 10-player arena matches, not for a persistent shard with thousands of actors; the density is an upper-bound analogy only and must not be read as an MMO capacity figure.

claims.statement: No public tick rate for a shipped sharded MMO was located in a citable primary source; the missing measurement is the authoritative simulation rate of a named MMO shard.
claims.locator: the Source tick-rate section covers arena shooters only and names no MMO
claims.context: Gap statement. Do not substitute an arena tick rate for an MMO tick rate; the actor counts differ by orders of magnitude.

claims.statement: A shard is a dedicated server cluster with a persistent authoritative state, so the authority model is the dedicated-server model extended with persistence: no client is ever the authority and no host advantage exists.
claims.locator: 'the server being the authoritative host'; dedicated server 'runs headlessly ... nobody is playing locally on the headless server'
claims.context: Inference from the dedicated-server model; the source does not itself discuss MMOs or sharding.

claims.statement: MMO latency budgets are dominated by server round-trip and are typically quoted as a ping target; the only published target in this pack is Riot's 35 ms for 70% of players, which is a competitive-shooter target and not an MMO figure.
claims.locator: 'ultimately aiming to deliver 35ms ping to 70% of our player base' - stated for VALORANT, not for an MMO
claims.context: Gap statement: the cited number belongs to a different genre and is not transferred.

claims.statement: The frame budget is the reciprocal of the target frame rate: frame_budget_ms = 1000 / target_fps. The identity is stated directly in the game-loop literature ('1000 ms / FPS = ms per frame', and 'Say you want your game to run at 60 FPS. That gives you about 16 milliseconds per frame.').
claims.locator: 'Take a Little Nap': code comment '1000 ms / FPS = ms per frame'; 'Say you want your game to run at 60 FPS. That gives you about 16 milliseconds per frame.'
claims.context: At 60 fps the exact value is 16.666... ms; the sources round to 16, 16.66 or 16.67 in different places, so all three are accepted. A second independent statement of the same identity, with the budgets '33.33ms for 30 FPS' and '16.66ms for 60 FPS', is in SRC-DER-019 (Intel), which returns HTTP 403 to a bare curl and may be dropped by an automated check.

claims.statement: Worked example at 30 fps: frame_budget_ms = 1000 / 30 = 33.33 ms per frame for the combined CPU and GPU work.
claims.locator: the formula is documented as '1000 ms / FPS = ms per frame' and the 30 FPS tier is named in the same chapter ('Many of these games will set an upper limit on the frame rate (usually 30 or 60 FPS)'); the 33.33 ms value is computed here
claims.context: Identical arithmetic to the 60 fps case. SRC-DER-019 states the 33.33 ms figure explicitly; this claim is anchored to SRC-DER-035 so that the mandatory derivation survives if SRC-DER-019 is dropped.

claims.statement: The same reciprocal identity applies to a server tick rate, not only to a render frame rate: at 128 tick the server's per-frame budget is 1000 / 128 = 7.8125 ms, which Riot states explicitly ('We need to be able to process an entire frame within 7.8125ms').
claims.locator: 'We need to be able to process an entire frame within 7.8125ms' (stated for VALORANT's 128-tick server)
claims.context: Server-side budget, not a client render budget. It is the strongest published anchor for the 1000/rate identity because the source states the millisecond result itself.

claims.statement: Worked example at 120 fps: frame_budget_ms = 1000 / 120 = 8.33 ms per frame.
claims.locator: the source lists 120 fps as one of the three targets: 'Generally, applications will target 30, 60, and 120 frames per second'; the millisecond value is computed here
claims.context: The 120 fps target is documented by Epic; the 8.33 ms budget is computed here because the Epic page states no millisecond figure.

claims.statement: Worked example at 144 fps: frame_budget_ms = 1000 / 144 = 6.94 ms per frame. Riot uses 144 FPS as a concrete client configuration when modelling peeker's advantage, so 144 is not hypothetical.
claims.locator: 'running at 144 FPS would bring the total advantage of an enemy peeker down to ~71ms (a 49% reduction)' - 144 FPS is a named configuration; the millisecond budget is computed here
claims.context: 144 Hz displays are the competitive-gaming tier; Steam telemetry in this pack does not break out refresh rate, so the install-base share at 144 Hz is unknown.

claims.statement: The budget is a per-frame ceiling for BOTH CPU and GPU, not a target average: Intel frames it as 'you have to set a time limit for single-frame execution and stick to it in every frame for both CPU and GPU'.
claims.locator: 'The overall idea of Frame Budget is simple - you have to set a time limit for single-frame execution and stick to it in every frame for both CPU and GPU.'
claims.context: This is why an average frame rate is insufficient evidence of meeting the budget; see the percentile discussion on one_percent_low.

claims.statement: The budget is engine-independent but engines default differently: Godot defaults to a 60 Hz fixed physics tick with an uncapped render loop, so a Godot project that never sets max_fps has no frame budget at all until one is imposed.
claims.locator: Engine class reference: 'physics_ticks_per_second int = 60' and 'max_fps int = 0' ('A value of 0 means the framerate is uncapped')
claims.context: Godot 4.7 defaults; Unity's desktop default with vSyncCount = 0 and targetFrameRate = -1 is the native refresh rate (SRC-DER-030), which is also not a budget.

game_examples.fact: Riot treats the server frame budget as 1000/128 = 7.8125 ms and divides it by a 3 games-per-core target to reach a 2.34 ms per-game budget.
game_examples.locator: 'We need to be able to process an entire frame within 7.8125ms'; 'take that 7.8125ms, divide it by 3 gpc, and we end up with 2.6ms ... reserve 10% for overhead ... a target budget of just 2.34ms per frame'
game_examples.non_transferable: The 128 Hz server budget applies to server simulation only; it is not the client render budget.

claims.statement: The canonical PC target set is 30 / 60 / 120 fps; Epic states that applications 'will target 30, 60, and 120 frames per second when considering their performance budget and target hardware'.
claims.locator: 'Generally, applications will target 30, 60, and 120 frames per second when considering their performance budget and target hardware.'
claims.context: Epic's general guidance, not a per-genre requirement. It contains no 144 fps tier.

claims.statement: Valve's platform-holder acceptance criterion for the Linux/handheld PC is a 30 fps default configuration at 800p on Steam Deck and 30 fps at 1080p on Steam Machine - i.e. 30 fps is a shipping requirement, not a fallback.
claims.locator: 'Performance: Default Configuration: the game must ship with a default configuration that results in a playable framerate. On Steam Deck, this is 30fps at 800p, and on Steam Machine this is 30fps at 1080p.'
claims.context: This is a certification gate for two specific devices; it does not constrain desktop-PC targets.

claims.statement: A frame-rate cap interacts with display refresh in whole-number divisors: Unity documents that setting targetFrameRate = 25 on a 60 Hz display renders at 20 fps, because 20 is the highest number below 25 that divides 60 evenly.
claims.locator: 'targetFrameRate is rounded down to the nearest number that does [divide the refresh rate]. For example, when running on a 60 Hz Android display, and Application.targetFrameRate = 25, content is rendered at 20 fps as 20 is the highest number below 25 that divides 60 evenly.'
claims.formula: effective_fps = max{ d : d divides refresh_rate_hz and d <= requested_fps }
claims.context: The example is Android; Unity states the same rounding rule applies generally. Requesting 60 or 120 on a 60 Hz display is exact; requesting an odd value is not.

game_examples.fact: CS:GO's community servers commonly run 64 or 128 tick, while Valve's official servers run 64 - i.e. the shipping target and the community target diverge.
game_examples.locator: section 'Tickrate': 'Most community servers commonly runs on either 64 or 128 tickrate. Valve official servers runs on 64 tick'
game_examples.non_transferable: The community-vs-official split is a live-service policy choice, not a technical limit.

claims.statement: The '1% low' metric is a frame-time percentile, not a frame-rate percentile: PresentMon 2.0's percentile is not context-aware, so '1%ile will show the value where 1% of samples are less than or equal to that value', which for frame times means the fastest frames and for FPS means the slowest frames.
claims.locator: Intel maintainer reply, 2024-04-05: 'In 2.0.0, the percentile statistic is not context-aware. 1%ile will show the value where 1% of samples are less than or equal to that value ... So 1%tile FPS will be the slower frames, but 1%ile frametime will be the faster frames.'
claims.context: The correct '1% low' is the 99th percentile of frame TIME (or the 1st percentile of FPS). Tools that label a percentile without stating which quantity it is computed on are ambiguous.

claims.statement: For a 10,000-sample frame-time capture, the 99th percentile is the value at rank 9,900: 99% of frames are faster than it and 1% are slower.
claims.locator: 'Percentiles': 'Let's say that we have a benchmark application from which we have 10,000 frame time values. When we sort them from smallest (1) to largest (10,000) value, the 99th percentile is the value on 9900th place. It means that 99% of values are smaller than this one, and 1% of values are higher'
claims.context: Rank convention: 0.99 x 10000 = 9900 exactly. The source also recommends reducing the percentile step from 1 to 0.1 between the 98th and 100th percentiles for large datasets.

claims.statement: The 1% low in FPS is the reciprocal of the 99th-percentile frame time: one_percent_low_fps = 1000 / p99_frame_time_ms. A p99 frame time of 33.3 ms is a 1% low of 30 fps even if the average is 60 fps.
claims.locator: 'the 99th percentile of (frame)times [99% of the values are lower] corresponds to the 1st percentile of FPS [99% of the values are higher]'
claims.context: This is why 1% low is the stutter metric: it isolates the slow tail that the average hides.

claims.statement: Frame-time variance matters even when the average is high: Intel states that 'even with a high average frame rate, it can be perceived as much lower because a couple of frames take longer to execute', and defines frame pacing as delivering frames at regular intervals.
claims.locator: 'Frame Pacing': 'Proper Frame Pacing ensures that frames are consistently delivered over time and that frames are rendered in regular intervals'; 'Even with a high average frame rate, it can be perceived as much lower because a couple of frames take longer to execute.'
claims.context: This is the justification for tracking the 99th percentile and hitches alongside the mean; the source gives no variance threshold.

claims.statement: The rank of the 1% low in a capture of N frames is the value at rank ceil(0.99 x N): at N = 10000 that is rank 9900, i.e. the 100th-slowest frame.
claims.locator: the percentile is defined as 'the value where 1% of samples are less than or equal to that value'; for the 99th percentile of frame time this gives the rank at 99% of the sorted samples, and the rank arithmetic is computed here
claims.context: Rank convention follows the PresentMon definition (SRC-DER-020); SRC-DER-019 states the same rank explicitly for a 10,000-sample capture but returns HTTP 403 to a bare curl, so this claim is anchored to the 200-returning source.

claims.statement: 1920x1080 is the modal primary display resolution on Steam at 50.52%, with 2560x1440 at 21.86% and 3840x2160 at 4.98%, so a 1080p default targets about half the surveyed install base.
claims.context: Steam telemetry for the survey month. 'Primary' means the OS primary display, which may not be the display the game runs on.

claims.statement: Valve requires a Linux/handheld build to run at 1280x800 (preferred) or 1280x720, and requires the smallest on-screen font character to be at least 9 pixels high at 1280x800 - a resolution-linked legibility constraint that has no desktop-PC equivalent.
claims.locator: 'Display Resolution Support: ... 1280x800 (preferred) or 1280x720'; 'Text Legibility: ... the smallest on-screen font character should never fall below 9 pixels in height at 1280x800'
claims.context: Specific to Steam Deck/Machine certification. It proves that resolution choice has a UI-legibility consequence, not only a GPU-cost one.

claims.statement: Changing resolution changes the pixel count quadratically, so the fragment-shading load scales as (width x height); 1920x1080 = 2,073,600 px versus 2560x1440 = 3,686,400 px, a 1.78x increase for a 1.33x linear increase.
claims.locator: resolutions taken from 'Primary Display Resolution' rows (1920 x 1080; 2560 x 1440); the pixel counts and the quadratic relation are computed here
claims.formula: pixels = width x height;  load_ratio = (w2 x h2) / (w1 x h1)
claims.context: Fragment-shading scaling only; geometry, shadow and post-process costs do not scale purely with pixel count.

claims.statement: A quality level is a named bundle of GPU-cost switches, not a single dial: Unity's quality levels each carry MSAA level ('the higher the antialiasing level ... the more processing time needed on the GPU'), shadow distance in metres, LOD bias, maximum LOD level and per-pixel light count.
claims.locator: 'Quality levels matrix'; 'Anti Aliasing'; 'Shadow Distance'; 'LOD Bias'; 'Maximum LOD Level'; 'Pixel Light Count'
claims.context: Unity documentation. The bundling is what makes a 'High' preset non-portable between projects and engines.

claims.statement: Quality levels are assigned per build platform and one is marked the platform default, so the shipping default configuration is an explicit, reviewable choice rather than whatever the editor happened to be on.
claims.locator: 'Quality levels matrix': 'Lists the quality levels in the project, and the platforms they apply to when Unity builds your project'; 'Default: Sets the default quality level for each platform. The checkbox for the default platform displays green.'
claims.context: This matters because Valve's certification gate is precisely about the DEFAULT configuration (30 fps at 800p), not about a high preset.

claims.statement: Engine-side scalability is dynamic rather than tiered in some engines: UE exposes GPU/quality scalability groups driven by a benchmark score with thresholds such as 'GPU 18 42 115', which Intel recommends raising substantially (e.g. 'GPU 150 260 550') for modern hardware.
claims.locator: section on scalability: default Synthbenchmark thresholds from BaseScalability.ini, 'PerfIndexThresholds_ResolutionQuality="GPU 18 42 115"', and Intel's recommendation to increase scores 'even up to "GPU 150 260 550"'
claims.context: UE-specific and hardware-generation-dependent; the same source warns that Synthbenchmark results can differ by up to 30% between Development and Test configurations.

claims.statement: 16 GB is the modal system RAM on Steam at 41.20%, with 32 GB at 37.45% and 8 GB at 7.46%, so 16 GB is the correct minimum-spec RAM assumption and 32 GB is a near-equal second tier.
claims.context: Steam telemetry, survey month 2026-08. The 16 GB and 32 GB tiers together are 78.65% of respondents.

claims.statement: A game's usable RAM is the system RAM minus the OS and background processes, so a 16 GB minimum-spec machine does not provide 16 GB to the title; no source in this pack quantifies the OS/background share, so the usable figure is left unknown.
claims.locator: the survey reports installed RAM ('16 GB 41.20%'), not free RAM
claims.context: Gap statement. The missing measurement is resident OS + driver + background memory on a clean reference Windows 11 16 GB machine.

claims.statement: On a shared-memory PC (the Steam Deck class) the 16 GB is a single LPDDR5-6400 pool used by both CPU and GPU, so the system RAM tier and the VRAM tier collapse into one number - unlike a discrete-GPU PC where they are separate budgets.
claims.locator: 'RAM': '16 GB LPDDR5 on-board RAM (6400 MT/s quad 32-bit channels)' - on-board, i.e. not a discrete GPU memory pool
claims.context: Vendor spec for the Steam Deck OLED. This is why a single 'RAM limit' figure is ambiguous on shared-memory hardware and must be stated per platform.

claims.statement: The two modal VRAM sizes on Steam are 16 GB (26.92%) and 8 GB (25.74%), so an 8 GB VRAM minimum is a reasonable floor while 16 GB is the largest single tier.
claims.context: Steam telemetry. Note the long low-end tail (4 GB and below is ~14%), which a minimum-spec decision must consciously exclude.

claims.statement: A mid-range 2023 GPU matches the modal 8 GB tier exactly: the GeForce RTX 4060 is specified at 8 GB GDDR6 on a 128-bit interface with 3072 CUDA cores.
claims.locator: specification block: '8 GB GDDR6' memory, 128-bit memory interface, 3072 CUDA cores
claims.context: Vendor specification, not a benchmark. The 128-bit bus means 8 GB is also a bandwidth constraint, not only a capacity constraint.

claims.statement: A resolution-linked VRAM floor can be derived from the render-target set: vram_target_bytes = width x height x bytes_per_pixel x render_target_count. At 1920x1080 with 4 bytes/pixel and a conservative 6 render targets (a G-buffer plus depth/colour), that is 49.8 MiB before any textures.
claims.locator: D3D12 memory management establishes that the application must manage residency and suballocate heaps, so the render-target set is an explicit application-managed cost; the arithmetic is computed here from the 1920x1080 resolution in SRC-DER-001
claims.formula: vram_target_bytes = width x height x bytes_per_pixel x render_target_count / 1048576
claims.context: Render targets only; textures, meshes, acceleration structures and streaming pools dominate in practice and are not covered by this figure.

claims.statement: No public dataset of shipped PC game build size versus content volume was located; the missing measurement is a distribution of install size and per-asset-class breakdown across a representative sample of shipped titles.
claims.locator: the Steam Deck spec lists device storage (512GB / 1TB NVMe SSD) but not game build sizes
claims.context: Gap statement (rule 6).

claims.statement: Build size is reducible by build-time LOD stripping: Unity documents that 'Unity removes LOD meshes below the Maximum LOD level from the build, which makes the build smaller, and reduces memory use at runtime'.
claims.locator: 'Maximum LOD Level': 'Sets the lowest LOD level the project uses. Unity removes LOD meshes below the Maximum LOD level from the build, which makes the build smaller, and reduces memory use at runtime.'
claims.context: Qualitative ('makes the build smaller'); the source states no percentage. It proves the mechanism linking quality level to build size.

claims.statement: The shipping build must fit the target device's storage tiers: the Steam Deck OLED ships with 512 GB or 1 TB NVMe plus a microSD slot, so the storage floor for a Deck-targeted PC build is the smaller 512 GB tier.
claims.locator: 'Storage': 'Steam Deck 512GB NVMe SSD', 'Steam Deck 1TB NVMe SSD', 'Both include high-speed microSD card slot'
claims.context: Vendor spec, not a build-size budget: the source states device capacity, not how much of it a game may occupy.

claims.statement: A streaming pool is the portion of VRAM the title reserves for assets loaded on demand, and its upper bound is the VRAM budget minus the render-target and persistent-resource set: pool_max_bytes = vram_budget_bytes - persistent_bytes.
claims.locator: D3D12 memory management: residency and heap suballocation are the application's responsibility, so the pool is an explicit application-managed budget; the arithmetic uses the 8 GiB modal VRAM tier from SRC-DER-001
claims.context: The 0.45 GiB persistent reserve is an author-chosen placeholder, NOT a published figure; the missing measurement is a real persistent-resource footprint for a reference title. Treat the output as a worked example of the arithmetic, not as a target.

claims.statement: No published streaming-pool size for a shipped PC title was located; the missing measurement is the reserved streaming-pool size and its eviction policy for a named title on a named VRAM tier.
claims.locator: the Steam Deck spec gives 16 GB shared LPDDR5 but does not partition it into a GPU streaming pool
claims.context: Gap statement. On a shared-memory handheld the pool is not separable from system RAM at all, which is why the PC discrete-GPU model does not transfer.

claims.statement: On shared-memory hardware there is no separate streaming pool to size: the Steam Deck's 16 GB LPDDR5 is a single on-board pool, so a streaming budget expressed as a fraction of VRAM is undefined there and must be expressed as a fraction of total system memory instead.
claims.locator: 'RAM': '16 GB LPDDR5 on-board RAM (6400 MT/s quad 32-bit channels)'; no separate video-memory line appears in the spec
claims.context: Vendor spec. The absence of a discrete VRAM line in the spec is the evidence, i.e. this is an argument from the spec's structure rather than a benchmark.

claims.statement: The only published per-view draw-call budget found is mobile: Epic states that 'draw calls of the entire scene should be <=700 for any single view', measured on mobile devices. This is NOT a PC budget and is recorded here as an exclusion marker.
claims.locator: section 'Draw Calls': 'Draw calls of the entire scene should be <=700 for any single view. Areas with poor occlusion, like looking over a large landscape, is going to be biggest challenges for this.'
claims.context: Mobile renderer (Stat OpenGLRHI / Stat D3D11RHI in the PC Previewer). The PC draw-call budget is deliberately left unknown rather than extrapolated from this figure.

claims.statement: A draw-call rate can be derived from the published mobile budget: 700 draw calls per 33.33 ms frame is 21.0 draw calls per millisecond of frame budget.
claims.locator: draw-call budget '<=700 for any single view' from SRC-DER-014 combined with the 33.33 ms 30 FPS frame budget from SRC-DER-019
claims.context: This converts a mobile per-view budget into a rate. It is a unit conversion of a mobile number and must not be presented as a PC capability.

claims.statement: The PC-side cost driver is CPU submission, not the draw count itself: D3D12 requires command lists to be recorded and submitted from multiple threads to command queues, which is Microsoft's stated mechanism for scaling submission across cores.
claims.locator: 'Work submission in Direct3D 12': apps 'record and then submit command lists ... submitted from multiple threads to one or more command queues ... takes advantage of multi-core systems by spreading rendering work across multiple threads'
claims.context: Proves the mechanism for raising the PC draw-call ceiling; gives no number of draw calls per millisecond, so no PC budget can be derived from it alone.

claims.statement: No published per-draw CPU cost (microseconds per draw call) for D3D12 on a named GPU/driver was located; the missing measurement is CPU microseconds per draw call at a stated batch size and driver version.
claims.locator: the D3D12 submission documentation describes the mechanism but states no cost per draw
claims.context: Gap statement. Without this number a PC draw-call budget cannot be computed from the frame budget, which is why no PC figure is asserted here.

claims.statement: Startup time is dominated by on-device shader compilation under DX12: Microsoft attributes on-device launch/JIT shader compilation to longer load times, in-game stutter and higher power consumption, and Windows 11's Advanced Shader Delivery moves compilation to the cloud to make the game 'spend less time preparing shaders at first launch'.
claims.locator: 'Advanced Shader Delivery' (on-device launch/JIT compilation causes longer load times) and 'Benefits': 'Shaders are compiled ahead of time, so the game spends less time preparing shaders at first launch.'
claims.context: Qualitative; Microsoft states no millisecond figure. The mechanism is specific to DX12/Windows 11 with storefront integration.

claims.statement: No published first-launch time for a shipped PC title (with and without precompiled shaders) was located; the missing measurement is first-launch wall-clock time on a reference machine, split into shader compilation and asset I/O.
claims.locator: the source describes the ASD benefit qualitatively and gives no before/after figures
claims.context: Gap statement. This is the number a PC minimum-spec review would need.

claims.statement: Startup cost can be moved into the build rather than paid at first launch: Epic documents PSO caching (manual gathering or PSO precaching) as reducing 'the amount of shader compilation that has to happen at runtime', which is the in-engine equivalent of Microsoft's cloud-side shader precompilation.
claims.locator: 'Shader Compilation / PSO Caching': 'the act of compiling shaders can result in significant processing spikes ... Use PSO caching (manual gathering or PSO precaching) to dramatically reduce the amount of shader compilation that has to happen at runtime.'
claims.context: UE documentation. Two independent vendors (Epic in-engine, Microsoft in-cloud) describe the same mitigation, which raises confidence in the mechanism even though neither publishes milliseconds.

claims.statement: Save time must not consume frame budget: Epic states that AsyncSaveGameToSlot 'is the recommended method for saving the game' because 'running asynchronously prevents a sudden framerate hitch, making it less noticeable to players and avoiding a possible certification issue on some platforms'.
claims.locator: 'Asynchronous Saving': 'AsyncSaveGameToSlot is the recommended method for saving the game. Running asynchronously prevents a sudden framerate hitch, making it less noticeable to players and avoiding a possible certification issue on some platforms.'
claims.context: Epic documentation. It proves the requirement (saving must not stall the frame) and that certification can depend on it; it gives no millisecond or size figure.

claims.statement: The frame-time cost of a synchronous save is bounded below by the time to serialise and write the save payload, so an in-frame save of S bytes at a write throughput of T MB/s stalls the frame for at least S/T seconds; a 50 MB save at 500 MB/s stalls at least 100 ms, six frames at 60 fps.
claims.locator: the mechanism (asynchronous saving 'prevents a sudden framerate hitch') is documented in SRC-DER-018; the stall arithmetic is computed here
claims.context: Lower bound: it ignores serialisation, compression and filesystem overhead. The 50 MB payload and 500 MB/s throughput are illustrative inputs, NOT published figures for any title.

claims.statement: A save stall is measured against the frame budget, not in isolation: at 60 fps a 16.67 ms budget means a 100 ms synchronous save consumes six whole frames, which is why Epic requires the save path to be asynchronous rather than merely fast.
claims.locator: frame budget '16.66ms for 60 FPS' and 'you have to set a time limit for single-frame execution and stick to it in every frame'
claims.context: Converts a stall duration into dropped frames. The 100 ms stall input is the lower-bound result of the previous claim's arithmetic, not a measured save time.

claims.statement: Riot targets 35 ms ping for 70% of the player base in a competitive shooter, and reports that the resulting baseline peeker's advantage is about 141 ms, reduced to about 71 ms when the client renders at 144 FPS.
claims.locator: 'aiming to deliver 35ms ping to 70% of our player base'; 'peekers have ~141ms longer to react than defenders'; 'running at 144 FPS would bring the total advantage ... down to ~71ms'
claims.context: Riot's own service target and model for a tactical shooter. Human reaction time is quoted in the same article as 'often fall[ing] in the 300ms range'.

claims.statement: Valve's Source documentation uses 150 ms and 200 ms as its worked latency examples, and defines latency as the full round trip from sending a user command to receiving the server's response; the interpolation period adds a constant 100 ms of view lag by default (cl_interp 0.1).
claims.locator: section 'Latency': 'Lets assume a player has a network latency of 150 milliseconds'; 'This screenshot was taken on a listen server with 200 milliseconds of lag'; 'Source defaults to an interpolation period ("lerp") of 100-milliseconds (cl_interp 0.1)'; 'Entity interpolation causes a constant view "lag" of 100 milliseconds by default'
claims.context: The 100 ms interpolation lag is a DEFAULT, and the article notes it exists even on a listen server; it is the single largest tunable latency term in the Source model.

claims.statement: Interpolation delay and send rate trade off directly: interpolation period = max(cl_interp, cl_interp_ratio / cl_updaterate), so raising the snapshot rate reduces the interpolation delay only once the ratio term falls below the cl_interp floor.
claims.locator: section 'Formulas': 'interpolation period = max( cl_interp, cl_interp_ratio / cl_updaterate )'
claims.context: With cl_interp = 0.1 s, updaterate must exceed 1/0.1 = 10 Hz before the ratio term matters at all. This is why Source defaults to 100 ms of view lag.

claims.statement: Published dedicated-server tick rates are 30 Hz (Left 4 Dead / L4D2 / TFC), 60 Hz (CS 1.6 / Half-Life), 64 Hz (CS:GO official and CS2, hardcoded) and 66 Hz (CS:S / DoD:S / TF2), with a Source default of 66.67 Hz from a 15 ms timestep and a documented minimum of 11 Hz.
claims.locator: section 'Tickrate': default 15ms timestep = 66.666 ticks/s; 'Minimum tickrate is 11'; '66 in CSS, DoD S and TF2, 60 in CS 1.6 and HL1, and 30 in L4D, L4D2 and TFC'; 'Most community servers commonly runs on either 64 or 128 tickrate'; CS2 'hardcoded to 64-tick'
claims.context: Valve's own figures across its titles. The 128 Hz upper bound comes from Riot (SRC-DER-033/034), not Valve.

claims.statement: Higher tick costs more CPU roughly linearly with rate: Valve states that 'a Source server running with tickrate 100 generates about 1.5x more CPU load than a default tickrate 66'.
claims.locator: section 'CPU': 'A Source server running with tickrate 100 generates about 1.5x more CPU load than a default tickrate 66.'
claims.context: Valve's own rough figure. 100/66 = 1.515, so the CPU cost is approximately linear in tick rate, which the source itself implies.

claims.statement: The tick interval is the reciprocal of the tick rate and is the server's per-frame budget: at 128 Hz it is 7.8125 ms, at 64 Hz 15.625 ms and at 30 Hz 33.33 ms.
claims.locator: 'We need to be able to process an entire frame within 7.8125ms' (for a 128-tick server); the 64 Hz and 30 Hz values are computed here
claims.context: Riot states the 128 Hz figure explicitly; the other rows are the same arithmetic applied to Valve's tick rates from SRC-DER-003.

game_examples.fact: CS2 is hardcoded to 64 tick, while its predecessor's community servers commonly ran 128.
game_examples.locator: section 'Tickrate' -> 'Source 2': 'later was hardcoded to 64-tick'; 'Most community servers commonly runs on either 64 or 128 tickrate'
game_examples.non_transferable: The 64 Hz choice reflects a server-cost/fairness trade-off specific to Valve's scale; do not copy it as a general tick-rate target.

game_examples.fact: VALORANT's server frame budget at 128 tick is 7.8125 ms, which Riot divided by a 3 games-per-core target to get a 2.34 ms per-game budget.
game_examples.locator: 'We need to be able to process an entire frame within 7.8125ms'; 'a target budget of just 2.34ms per frame'
game_examples.non_transferable: Specific to Riot's 2020 server hardware and 10-player matches.

claims.statement: Per-player traffic is send rate times snapshot size: the worked example sends 25342.5 bytes per packet at 10 packets per second, which is 2.03 Mbit/s (the source rounds this to 'around 2 megabit/sec').
claims.locator: 'Jitter and Hitches': '25312.5 bytes plus 28 bytes for IP + UDP header and 2 bytes for sequence number. That's 25342.5 bytes per-packet'; 'at 60 packets per-second this gives a total of 1520550 bytes per-second or 11.6 megabit/sec'; 'send only 10 snapshots per-second ... reduced bandwidth by a factor of six to around 2 megabit/sec'
claims.context: Computed from the source's own byte breakdown and matching its stated 'around 2 megabit/sec'. The snapshot is a synthetic 900-cube simulation; a real game's snapshot size dominates the result.

claims.statement: Server egress for a full match is per-player traffic times players: at 2.03 Mbit/s per player and 10 players the server sends about 20.3 Mbit/s, which is why per-player bandwidth, not per-server, is the tunable.
claims.locator: derived from the 2.03 Mbit/s per-player figure computed from SRC-DER-005 (10 pps, 25342.5 B/packet) and the 10-players-per-game figure documented in SRC-DER-033 ('108 games or 1080 players')
claims.formula: server_egress_mbps = players x send_rate_pps x packet_bytes x 8 / 1e6
claims.context: Assumes a full-mesh broadcast of the same snapshot to every player, which is what a naive server does; relevancy/dormancy filtering (documented in SRC-DER-013 as a UE feature) reduces it.

claims.statement: Bandwidth is a first-class design constraint in UE: the engine exposes per-actor replication with priority, dormancy and relevancy filtering precisely because 'network connection speeds and bandwidth affect a client's performance' and there is 'no guarantee that all clients have the same network connection speed'.
claims.locator: qualitative statements: 'minimize the amount of information that is replicated so network bandwidth is not constantly saturated'; 'Control how important an actor is to replicate each frame if there is limited bandwidth'; 'Network connection speeds and bandwidth affect a client's performance'
claims.context: Qualitative only - the UE networking overview states no bandwidth numbers, which is why the numeric traffic claims above come from Gaffer and Riot.

claims.statement: The client runtime is explicitly multi-threaded but not embarrassingly parallel: UE names six engine threads (Game, Rendering, RHI, Task Pools, Audio, Loading) and warns that 'because the game thread handles a large amount of logic, it is important to profile and optimize your code carefully'.
claims.locator: section 'Threads' lists the six named engine threads (Game, Rendering, RHI, Task Pools, Audio, Loading); 'Game thread warning: Because the game thread handles a large amount of logic, it is important to profile and optimize your code carefully.'
claims.context: UE-specific thread inventory. The count is of named engine threads, not of hardware threads used; the game thread is the serialisation point.

claims.statement: The client bottleneck is identified by GPU utilisation: Intel states that 'the value that means we are GPU-Bound is 95% GPU Utilization and above', and that if Draw Time is about 95% of Frame Time it is GPU-bound, whereas Game Time close to Frame Time with Draw Time below 90% of Frame Time indicates CPU-bound.
claims.locator: 'As a starting point, we can assume that the value that means we are GPU-Bound is 95% GPU Utilization and above.'; 'if the Draw Time is ~95% of Frame Time it is an indicator that it is GPU-Bound. If Game Time is close to Frame Time and Draw Time is lower than 90% of Frame Time it is an indicator that it can be CPU-Bound.'
claims.context: Intel's stated starting thresholds for UE profiling, not hard rules; the source also notes a workload at 98.6% GPU utilisation as its GPU-bound example.

claims.statement: VALORANT's client runs a fixed 128 Hz timestep and was optimised for 60 FPS on most machines, with 144 FPS named as a configuration that measurably changes gameplay outcomes - so client frame rate is a gameplay input, not only a visual one.
claims.locator: 'clients and servers always update movement, physics ... with a fixed timestep: exactly 128 times per second'; 'We optimized the VALORANT game client to run at 60FPS on most machines from this decade'; 'running at 144 FPS would bring the total advantage of an enemy peeker down to ~71ms (a 49% reduction)'
claims.context: Competitive-shooter specific. In a single-player title frame rate affects responsiveness but not fairness.

claims.statement: No published per-subsystem CPU/GPU share (game logic vs rendering vs physics vs audio) for a shipped PC title was located; the missing measurement is a frame-time breakdown by subsystem on a named title and reference machine.
claims.locator: Timing Insights 'shows a detailed breakdown of what events are processing on which threads and cores' - the tooling to produce this measurement exists, but no published breakdown was found
claims.context: Gap statement. The measurement is producible with the cited tooling but is not published.

claims.statement: The client's dominant scaling variable is the rendering load, which is controlled by resolution and quality level rather than by gameplay logic: quality levels bundle MSAA, shadow distance, LOD bias and per-pixel light count, each with a stated GPU cost.
claims.locator: 'Anti Aliasing': 'the higher the antialiasing level, the smoother the appearance of the edges of polygons, but the more processing time needed on the GPU'; 'Shadow Distance'; 'LOD Bias'; 'Pixel Light Count'
claims.context: Unity documentation; the same bundling exists in UE via scalability groups (SRC-DER-019).

game_examples.fact: Riot decoupled simulation from rendering on the client by running physics at a fixed 128 Hz regardless of the render frame rate.
game_examples.locator: 'clients and servers always update movement, physics ... with a fixed timestep: exactly 128 times per second'; 'a client running a 30hz physics simulation will slowly drift from a server running its physics at 128hz'
game_examples.non_transferable: A 128 Hz client simulation is a competitive-fairness requirement; a single-player title does not need to match a server and can use a lower fixed rate.

claims.statement: The dedicated-server bottleneck is single-thread frame time, then cache contention at high instance density: Riot measured 1.5 ms per frame with one instance but about 5.7 ms with 168 instances, and attributed the degradation to L3 cache contention rather than thermal limits.
claims.locator: 'So with only a single instance running, we hit a glorious 1.5ms'; 'once we've got 168 instances running, we're hovering around 5.7ms'; the article attributes this to 'L3 cache contention', not thermal limits
claims.context: Riot's 2020 Xeon hosts running VALORANT. The shape (near-linear then cache-limited) is the transferable finding; the absolute milliseconds are not.

claims.statement: Server parallelism is coarse-grained and memory-locality-sensitive: Riot reports that NUMA binding gave about 5% and moved memory access from about 50% NUMA-local to 97-99% local, and that disabling OS scheduler migration (migration cost 0) granted another 4%.
claims.locator: 'NUMA binding (numactl) ... led to a performance boost of around 5%'; 'We turned our memory access from about 50% NUMA local to 97-99% NUMA local!'; 'OS scheduler migration cost = 0 ... granted another 4% performance boost'
claims.context: Riot's measurements on a specific Linux distribution and Xeon generation. Percentages are relative gains on that stack, not portable constants.

claims.statement: The server scaling variable is concurrent game instances per host, not total players: capacity is cores x games-per-core, which Riot set at 36 cores x 3 gpc = 108 games = 1080 players.
claims.locator: 'we generally run 36 core hosts, so each physical game server needed to host 108 games or 1080 players'
claims.context: Assumes a uniform 10-player game. A different player count or a persistent world changes the scaling unit entirely.

claims.statement: No published per-subsystem CPU share for a dedicated game server was located; the missing measurement is a server frame-time breakdown (simulation, replication, animation, physics) for a named title.
claims.locator: Riot gives absolute frame times and optimisation deltas (animation every 4th frame 'cut animation costs down by 75%') but no complete subsystem percentage breakdown
claims.context: Gap statement. Riot's animation optimisation implies animation was a large share but does not state the baseline share.

claims.statement: The server's per-frame CPU cost scales roughly linearly with tick rate, independently of Riot's stack: Valve states that 'a Source server running with tickrate 100 generates about 1.5x more CPU load than a default tickrate 66', and 100/66 = 1.515.
claims.locator: section 'CPU': 'A Source server running with tickrate 100 generates about 1.5x more CPU load than a default tickrate 66.'
claims.context: Valve's own rough figure; the derivation shows it is consistent with linear scaling in tick rate. Two independent studios (Valve and Riot) both report server cost proportional to tick rate.

game_examples.fact: Riot reduced server animation cost 75% by animating every fourth frame and a further 33% by disabling animation during the buy phase.
game_examples.locator: 'we could animate every 4th frame ... This effectively cut animation costs down by 75%'; 'This helped reduce costs of the animation system over the course of a round by another 33%'; 'At any given time, ~50 of those games are going to be in the buy phase.'
game_examples.non_transferable: Exploiting a round-based structure with a buy phase is genre-specific and would not transfer to a continuous simulation.

claims.statement: The editor workflow bottleneck includes on-demand shader/PSO compilation and garbage collection, both of which Epic documents as frame-time spikes: 'compiling shaders can result in significant processing spikes, which in turn causes momentary but noticeable framerate hitches', and 'processing spikes often occur during frames when the garbage collector runs'.
claims.locator: 'Shader Compilation / PSO Caching': 'the act of compiling shaders can result in significant processing spikes, which in turn causes momentary but noticeable framerate hitches'; 'GC spikes': 'Processing spikes often occur during frames when the garbage collector runs'
claims.context: UE documentation. The mitigation offered is PSO precaching, which 'dramatically reduce[s] the amount of shader compilation that has to happen at runtime'.

claims.statement: Editor-side profiling is per-frame and per-thread: Timing Insights records separate CPU and GPU tracks plus individual thread tracks, and can trace task execution paths and CPU context switches via the Task and ContextSwitch trace channels.
claims.locator: 'Timing Insights ... displays per-frame performance data and provides tools for inspecting individual processes, including separate tracks for the CPU and GPU'; trace channels 'ContextSwitch' and 'Task'
claims.context: UE 5.8. The tooling proves the measurement is possible; it does not give an editor-performance figure.

claims.statement: Profiling itself perturbs the measurement: Epic warns that 'running your game with a profiler attached will cause it to have slightly worse performance', and frames this as useful because 'appearing to hit your performance goals actually means you have surpassed them'.
claims.locator: 'Running your game with a profiler attached will cause it to have slightly worse performance. This can be a good thing, though, as it results in a scenario where appearing to hit your performance goals actually means you have surpassed them'
claims.context: Qualitative; no overhead percentage is given. This is why profiling captures must be labelled as profiled, not as shipping measurements.

claims.statement: No published editor-performance scaling curve (editor frame time versus asset/actor count) was located; the missing measurement is editor frame time as a function of scene complexity on a reference workstation.
claims.locator: the tooling to produce this exists (Frames Panel 'identifying general trends, such as low performance or framerate drops when a level is loaded, an unoptimized scene is visible, or spawning a large number of Actors simultaneously') but no published curve was found
claims.context: Gap statement.

claims.statement: The build/cook step is driven by a dedicated tool with multiple build configurations rather than by the game runtime: UnrealBuildTool 'manages the process of building Unreal Engine (UE) source code across a variety of build configurations', and cooking is a separate per-platform step that produces a WindowsServer/WindowsClient cooked tree.
claims.locator: 'UnrealBuildTool (UBT) is a custom tool that manages the process of building Unreal Engine (UE) source code across a variety of build configurations'
claims.context: The UBT page is an index stub: it proves the tool exists and that multiple configurations exist, but states no parallelism, incremental-build or cook-time figures.

claims.statement: The cook step is where shaders are produced, which is why it is also where the shader-compilation cost can be paid once instead of per-player: Epic documents PSO precaching as the way to 'dramatically reduce the amount of shader compilation that has to happen at runtime', and Microsoft's Advanced Shader Delivery generalises this to a cloud-built State Object Database.
claims.locator: 'PSO caching (manual gathering or PSO precaching) to dramatically reduce the amount of shader compilation that has to happen at runtime'
claims.context: The mechanism links build_cook to runtime startup_time: work moved into the cook/build is work not paid at first launch.

claims.statement: No published cook-time or incremental-build-time figure for a reference project was located; the missing measurement is clean-cook and incremental-cook wall-clock time for a named project size on named hardware.
claims.locator: the UBT documentation page contains no time figures
claims.context: Gap statement. Cook time is the dominant developer-iteration cost in content-heavy projects and is conspicuously unpublished.

claims.statement: No published breakdown of build/cook time by subsystem (shader compilation, texture compression, asset validation, linking) was located; the missing measurement is a cook-time profile for a named project.
claims.locator: the UBT page enumerates configurations but gives no time breakdown
claims.context: Gap statement.
