claims.statement: The development workstation's memory requirement is not the shipping minimum: the modal Steam system has 16 GB RAM (41.20%) and 8 GB VRAM (25.74%), while an editor plus a cook plus a debug build runs several processes concurrently, so the shipping distribution understates the workstation need.
claims.context: Inference from the shipping-install distribution; the source measures player machines, NOT developer workstations, so it is a floor rather than a workstation recommendation.

claims.statement: The workstation workload is many-process and many-core: a build runs UBT across configurations while the editor and a debug game run simultaneously, and the engine itself already runs six named threads in the game process alone.
claims.locator: 'Threads' lists six named engine threads in the running game process (Game, Rendering, RHI, Task Pools, Audio, Loading)
claims.context: The six-thread figure is for the game process, not for the workstation as a whole; the workstation's aggregate parallelism is not published.

claims.statement: No published specification for a game-development workstation (core count, RAM, VRAM, storage) tied to a measured iteration time was located; the missing measurement is build/editor iteration time versus workstation specification.
claims.locator: UBT is documented as the build driver but the source states no hardware requirements
claims.context: Gap statement. This is the key missing input for any 'developer iteration speed' budget.

claims.statement: No published per-subsystem load profile (CPU vs GPU vs disk vs network) for a development workstation was located; the missing measurement is a whole-machine utilisation profile during a representative edit-build-test cycle.
claims.locator: Timing Insights profiles the game/editor process only, not the whole workstation
claims.context: Gap statement.

claims.statement: Scope creep is triggered whenever new features are accepted after the feature list is frozen, or when a team starts a second system and re-adds everything it deferred in the first - Brooks' 'second-system effect'.
claims.locator: 'The second-system effect proposes that, when an architect designs a second system, it is the most dangerous system they will ever design, because they will tend to incorporate all of the additions they originally did not add to the first system due to inherent time constraints.'
claims.context: Brooks (1975), via a secondary summary. The mechanism is qualitative; there is no published probability of scope creep.

claims.statement: The detection signal is milestone slippage accumulating one day at a time: Brooks writes 'How does a large software project get to be one year late? Answer: One day at a time!', so the signal is missed small milestones rather than a single large overrun.
claims.locator: 'Progress tracking': 'Question: How does a large software project get to be one year late? Answer: One day at a time!'; 'Incremental slippages on many fronts eventually accumulate to produce a large overall delay. Continued attention to meeting small individual milestones is required at each level of management.'
claims.context: Brooks (1975) via secondary summary. This is a detection heuristic, not a measurement.

claims.statement: The coordination cost of a growing team grows quadratically, which bounds how much scope a team can absorb: Brooks' 50-person example implies n(n-1)/2 = 1,225 communication channels, so adding people to absorb scope adds more coordination than capacity.
claims.locator: 'Communication': 50 people -> '1,225 channels of communication' (n(n-1)/2)
claims.context: Brooks' figure. The formula bounds coordination overhead, not productive capacity; it is the quantitative basis of Brooks' Law (see late_technology_adoption).

claims.statement: No published base rate for scope creep in game projects was located; the missing measurement is the incidence of post-freeze feature additions across a representative sample of shipped titles.
claims.locator: Brooks argues the mechanism but publishes no incidence rate
claims.context: Gap statement. The band is left qualitative ('high' by construction of the second-system effect) rather than numeric.

claims.statement: The cost of scope added after a phase boundary is set by the Boehm phase multiplier: a change made at design cost 3x-8x a requirements-phase change, at code 5x-20x, and at acceptance testing 30x-100x, so accepting scope after preproduction is an order-of-magnitude decision rather than an incremental one.
claims.locator: table 'Relative cost to fix one defect by the phase it is caught' (Boehm 1981): 'Design 3x to 8x', 'Code 5x to 20x', 'Test (acceptance / UAT) 30x to 100x'
claims.context: Boehm's defect-fix multiplier used as a proxy for the cost of adding scope by phase. The proxy is the author's construction; the ratios are Boehm's, via a secondary restatement, and vary by project type.

game_examples.fact: Anthem's post-launch soft reboot ('Anthem Next') was an attempt to re-scope the game after release and was ultimately abandoned.
game_examples.locator: 'a small group of developers at BioWare were working on a soft reboot of the game, referred to as Anthem Next'
game_examples.non_transferable: Attempting to re-scope after release is the most expensive form of scope change (operations-phase multiplier); it is not a substitute for freezing scope in beta.

claims.statement: Adopting a new engine or API version late in a project triggers a rewrite: Godot's own migration guide states the engine was 'rewritten in many aspects, some features have unfortunately been lost in the process', listing renamed methods/properties/signals, shader updates, and ArrayMesh resource compatibility breakage.
claims.locator: 'rewrite in many aspects, some features have unfortunately been lost in the process'; contents list 'List of automatically renamed methods, properties, signals and constants', 'Updating shaders', 'ArrayMesh resource compatibility breakage'; 'Bullet physics was removed in favor of GodotPhysics'
claims.context: Godot 3.x -> 4.x specifically. The mechanism (major-version breakage) generalises; the specific breakages do not.

claims.statement: Brooks' Law is the quantitative mitigation argument: 'adding manpower to a late software project makes it later', because new developers consume existing developers' time for onboarding - so a late technology switch cannot be recovered by staffing up.
claims.locator: 'Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later'; 'The central insight is that new developers require onboarding, which in turn requires time of existing developers' (paraphrase of the law's explanation)
claims.context: Brooks (1975) via secondary summary. The law is qualitative; no numeric throughput loss is published here.

claims.statement: The cost of a late change is bounded by the Boehm phase multiplier: a change made in alpha costs 10x-50x a requirements-phase change, and in beta 30x-100x, so a technology switch deferred past alpha is a schedule event of that magnitude.
claims.locator: table 'Relative cost to fix one defect by the phase it is caught' (Boehm 1981): 'Test (development) 10x to 50x', 'Test (acceptance / UAT) 30x to 100x'
claims.context: Boehm's multiplier is about DEFECT fixes by phase, applied here as a proxy for the cost of a late technology change. The proxy is the author's; the ratios are Boehm's (via a secondary restatement).

claims.statement: A practical detection signal is that the new technology's feature set is not a superset of the old one: Godot 4's removal of Bullet physics in favour of GodotPhysics is a documented capability regression that only becomes visible when the affected 3D projects are ported.
claims.locator: 'Bullet physics was removed in favor of GodotPhysics. This only affects 3D projects that used the default physics engine (which was Bullet) and didn't [override it]'
claims.context: Godot-specific example of the general signal: enumerate capabilities present in the old version and absent in the new one BEFORE committing to the switch.

game_examples.fact: Migrating a Godot 3 project to Godot 4 requires renaming methods/properties/signals/constants, updating shaders and resolving ArrayMesh resource breakage, and lost Bullet physics.
game_examples.locator: 'List of automatically renamed methods, properties, signals and constants'; 'Updating shaders'; 'ArrayMesh resource compatibility breakage'; 'Bullet physics was removed in favor of GodotPhysics'
game_examples.non_transferable: This is a specific 3.x->4.x migration list; do not generalise it to other engine version pairs without re-deriving the breakage list.

claims.statement: Content scale is systematically underestimated because product-grade content costs more than in-house content: Brooks states that 'programming products ... and programming systems are both three times as hard to write as simple independent in-house programs' (Figure 1.1, Page 13).
claims.locator: 'Project estimation': 'programming products (which can be sold to paying customers) and programming systems are both three times as hard to write as simple independent in-house programs [The Mythical Man-Month Figure 1.1, Page 13]'
claims.context: Brooks' 3x factor is for PROGRAMMING PRODUCTS, applied here as a proxy for shipped content. It is a 1975 estimate from OS/360 experience, via a secondary summary, and is not a measured game-content ratio.

claims.statement: The signal is that asset count grows while per-asset cost is assumed constant: Unity's quality model shows that a single LOD decision (Maximum LOD Level) changes build size and runtime memory, so content scale and content cost are coupled through the asset pipeline rather than independent.
claims.locator: 'Maximum LOD Level': 'Unity removes LOD meshes below the Maximum LOD level from the build, which makes the build smaller, and reduces memory use at runtime.'
claims.context: Weak signal, offered as a mechanism: the source proves the coupling but gives no per-asset cost.

claims.statement: The mitigation is a throw-away pilot: Brooks' 'pilot system' argues that a team designing a new kind of system will build a throw-away system whether it intends to or not, and that the second, smarter system is the one to deliver.
claims.locator: 'The pilot system': 'When designing a new kind of system, a team will design a throw-away system (whether it intends to or not) ... This second, smarter system should be the one delivered to the customer, since delivery of the pilot system would cause nothing but agony to the customer'
claims.context: Brooks (1975) via secondary summary. Budget the pilot as throw-away content, not as shippable content.

claims.statement: No published base rate for content-scale overruns in game projects was located; the missing measurement is the ratio of shipped to originally-planned asset counts across a sample of titles.
claims.locator: Brooks argues the estimation failure but publishes no incidence rate
claims.context: Gap statement.

claims.statement: The detection signal is frame-time spikes rather than a drop in average FPS: Timing Insights is built to 'determine which frames are experiencing spikes in required processing time' and the Frames panel identifies 'framerate drops when a level is loaded, an unoptimized scene is visible, or spawning a large number of Actors simultaneously'.
claims.locator: 'Determine which frames are experiencing spikes in required processing time'; Frames panel: 'identifying general trends, such as low performance or framerate drops when a level is loaded, an unoptimized scene is visible, or spawning a large number of Actors simultaneously'
claims.context: UE 5.8 tooling. This is why the regression gate must be on the 99th-percentile frame time, not the mean (see target_metrics.one_percent_low).

claims.statement: Known regression triggers are garbage-collection spikes and on-demand shader/PSO compilation: Epic documents that 'processing spikes often occur during frames when the garbage collector runs, especially if your application has destroyed a large number of objects recently' and that shader compilation 'causes momentary but noticeable framerate hitches'.
claims.locator: 'Processing spikes often occur during frames when the garbage collector runs, especially if your application has destroyed a large number of objects recently'; 'the act of compiling shaders can result in significant processing spikes, which in turn causes momentary but noticeable framerate hitches'
claims.context: UE-specific mechanisms, but the class of risk (a periodic or on-demand operation inside the frame) is general.

claims.statement: The mitigation is to move work off the frame or amortise it: Epic recommends asynchronous spawning spread over frames ('spawn only up to 5 enemies per frame' for 30 enemies over 6 frames) and PSO precaching to 'dramatically reduce the amount of shader compilation that has to happen at runtime'.
claims.locator: 'you could create an async operation to spawn only up to 5 enemies per frame until it has reached the specified limit'; 'This would result in all 30 enemies spawning over the course of 6 frames'; 'PSO caching ... dramatically reduce the amount of shader compilation that has to happen at runtime'
claims.context: The source's own worked example (30 enemies / 5 per frame / 6 frames), used as an illustration of amortisation; the specific numbers are not a recommendation.

claims.statement: No published regression rate (regressions per patch, or share of patches introducing a frame-time regression) for shipped PC titles was located; the missing measurement is an automated frame-time regression rate across a patch history.
claims.locator: the tooling to measure it is documented but no published rate was found
claims.context: Gap statement.

claims.statement: A platform API is deprecated on a vendor's schedule, not the project's: Steamworks states that ISteamNetworking is 'an older, deprecated API ... we may remove this API from the SDK in a future release', so any title built on it carries a forced-migration liability.
claims.locator: 'ISteamNetworking is an older, deprecated API. If you are using it, consider migrating to a newer API soon, as we may remove this API from the SDK in a future release.'
claims.context: Steamworks documentation, current at verification time. Deprecation is announced but removal has no published date.

claims.statement: The mitigation is to abstract the platform boundary, which is what the specification itself permits: Vulkan's ABI is 'platform- or implementation-defined' and applications 'should only rely on shared library symbols for commands in the minimum core version required', obtaining later entry points via vkGetInstanceProcAddr/vkGetDeviceProcAddr.
claims.locator: section 3.4 ABI: 'The mechanism by which Vulkan is made available to applications is platform- or implementation-defined'; 'Applications should only rely on shared library symbols for commands in the minimum core version required by the application. vkGetInstanceProcAddr and vkGetDeviceProcAddr should be used to obtain function pointers for commands in core versions beyond the application's minimum required version.'
claims.context: Vulkan specification guidance. Relying only on the minimum core version and resolving newer entry points dynamically is the specified pattern for surviving API growth.

claims.statement: The impact of an API break is bounded by the Boehm phase multiplier at the point of discovery: found in beta it is 30x-100x a requirements-phase change, found in production 50x-200x.
claims.locator: table 'Relative cost to fix one defect by the phase it is caught' (Boehm 1981): 'Test (acceptance / UAT) 30x to 100x'; 'Operations (production) 50x to 200x'
claims.context: Boehm's defect-fix multiplier used as a proxy for the cost of an API-break fix by phase. The proxy is the author's; the ratios are Boehm's (via a secondary restatement).

claims.statement: The detection signal is a documented capability or format change in the vendor's migration notes - e.g. Godot 4's 'ArrayMesh resource compatibility breakage' and the removal of Bullet physics - which must be enumerated before committing to the upgrade.
claims.locator: 'ArrayMesh resource compatibility breakage'; 'Bullet physics was removed in favor of GodotPhysics'
claims.context: Engine-version example of the general signal; the specific items are Godot 3->4 only.

claims.statement: A third-party dependency can be removed by the vendor itself: Godot 4 removed Bullet physics in favour of GodotPhysics, so a project that depended on the default (Bullet) physics engine had its dependency removed by an engine upgrade.
claims.locator: 'Bullet physics was removed in favor of GodotPhysics. This only affects 3D projects that used the default physics engine (which was Bullet) and didn't [override it]'
claims.context: Godot 3.x -> 4.x. It proves the class of risk (vendor-side dependency removal) with a concrete instance.

claims.statement: The mitigation is Brooks' 'specialized tools' guidance: rather than every programmer having their own tools, 'each team should have a designated tool-maker' and 'system-wide tools should be built by a common tools team, overseen by the project manager' - i.e. own the critical toolchain rather than depend on it.
claims.locator: 'Specialized tools': 'each team should have a designated tool-maker who may create tools that are highly customized for the job that team is doing'; 'system-wide tools should be built by a common tools team, overseen by the project manager'
claims.context: Brooks (1975) via secondary summary. Building an in-house tool is itself a dependency on your own maintenance capacity.

claims.statement: No published abandonment rate for game-development dependencies was located; the missing measurement is the survival rate of the third-party libraries in a shipped title's dependency list over a five-year window.
claims.locator: the source documents one removal but gives no rate
claims.context: Gap statement.

claims.statement: Multiplayer changes the authority model and therefore the whole architecture: UE distinguishes NM_Standalone / NM_DedicatedServer / NM_ListenServer / NM_Client, and 'most actors do not replicate by default', so retrofitting multiplayer requires reworking every gameplay system's state ownership.
claims.locator: 'Network Modes' enum NM_Standalone / NM_DedicatedServer / NM_ListenServer / NM_Client; 'most actors do not replicate by default'; three replication systems (Generic, Replication Graph, Iris)
claims.context: UE documentation. The 'do not replicate by default' default is the specific reason retrofitting is expensive.

claims.statement: The cost of adding multiplayer late is bounded by the phase multiplier at the point of the decision: a design-phase change is 3x-8x a requirements-phase change, while a beta-phase change is 30x-100x, so multiplayer scope decided after preproduction is an order-of-magnitude decision.
claims.locator: table 'Relative cost to fix one defect by the phase it is caught' (Boehm 1981): 'Design 3x to 8x'; 'Test (acceptance / UAT) 30x to 100x'
claims.context: Boehm's defect-fix multiplier used as a proxy for the cost of adding multiplayer by phase. The proxy is the author's; the ratios are Boehm's (via a secondary restatement).

claims.statement: The mitigation is to choose the authority model explicitly and early: a listen server is 'often acceptable for casual multiplayer and cooperative gaming' while a dedicated server is 'ideal for large-scale or competitive games', and the two impose different hosting, certification and anti-cheat obligations.
claims.locator: 'A listen server is often acceptable for casual multiplayer and cooperative gaming, but dedicated servers are ideal for large-scale or competitive games.'
claims.context: Epic's guidance. Choosing listen vs dedicated later is itself a late change, since it moves the authority boundary.

claims.statement: A concrete detection signal is that the relay/topology assumptions have not been made: Steamworks relays all P2P traffic by default and requires re-architecting 'any place where network hosts are identified by a public IP' to use a different identifier, so a design that still passes IPs around has not yet absorbed the multiplayer requirement.
claims.locator: 'any place where network hosts are identified by a public IP (almost always the case for gameservers) will need to be changed to use a different identifier instead'; 'All P2P connections are automatically relayed over the Valve backbone when appropriate'
claims.context: Steamworks SDR documentation. Specific to the Steam relay model.

game_examples.fact: Riot found that converting a replicated variable to an RPC 'offered a 100x to 10000x performance improvement', i.e. replication design choices dominate server cost.
game_examples.locator: 'changing from a replicated variable to an RPC offered a 100x to 10000x performance improvement!'
game_examples.non_transferable: A 100x-10000x range is an optimisation outcome on Riot's codebase, not a transferable constant; do not budget a 100x saving into a plan.

claims.statement: A tooling gap is triggered when the team must answer a question the shipped tools cannot answer, e.g. attributing a frame-time spike to a subsystem: Timing Insights answers per-thread CPU/GPU attribution, but the source itself scopes it to the game/editor process only.
claims.locator: 'Timing Insights ... displays per-frame performance data and provides tools for inspecting individual processes, including separate tracks for the CPU and GPU' - scope is the traced process
claims.context: The gap is between process-level profiling (available) and whole-system/workstation profiling (not provided by this tool).

claims.statement: The mitigation is to designate tool ownership: Brooks' 'specialized tools' argues for 'a designated tool-maker' per team and 'a common tools team' for system-wide tools, overseen by the project manager.
claims.locator: 'Specialized tools': 'each team should have a designated tool-maker ... In addition, system-wide tools should be built by a common tools team, overseen by the project manager.'
claims.context: Brooks (1975) via secondary summary. It is an organisational mitigation, not a technical one.

claims.statement: A detection signal is that profiling changes the thing being measured: Epic warns profiler attachment makes the game 'slightly worse', so a team that cannot distinguish profiled from unprofiled captures has a measurement-integrity gap, not only a tooling gap.
claims.locator: 'Running your game with a profiler attached will cause it to have slightly worse performance.'
claims.context: Qualitative; no overhead percentage is given, so the size of the perturbation is unknown.

claims.statement: No published incidence of tooling gaps in game projects was located; the missing measurement is the share of projects that build custom tooling and the schedule cost of doing so.
claims.locator: Brooks argues for tool-makers but publishes no incidence rate
claims.context: Gap statement.

claims.statement: Save compatibility breaks when the save payload schema changes between patches: Epic's save system serialises a USaveGame subclass to a named slot, so any change to that class's fields is a potential incompatibility with existing saves.
claims.locator: 'Creating a SaveGame Object' (USaveGame; 'The system supports the ability to have multiple saved game files, and to save different SaveGame classes'); saving to a named slot
claims.context: UE documentation. The source describes the mechanism but gives no versioning policy or migration guidance, so the compatibility contract is on the title.

claims.statement: The mitigation is to keep saving off the frame and to treat save writes as an asynchronous, versioned operation: Epic recommends AsyncSaveGameToSlot because running asynchronously 'prevents a sudden framerate hitch' and 'avoid[s] a possible certification issue on some platforms'.
claims.locator: 'AsyncSaveGameToSlot is the recommended method for saving the game. Running asynchronously prevents a sudden framerate hitch, making it less noticeable to players and avoiding a possible certification issue on some platforms.'
claims.context: Proves that save behaviour is a certification concern on some platforms, so save compatibility is not only a player-experience issue.

claims.statement: A concrete detection signal is the absence of an explicit code-freeze policy: Brooks' 'Code freeze and system versioning' argues that changing a system to meet changed user needs 'can only occur up to a certain point, otherwise the s[ystem never ships]', so a project without a versioning policy cannot reason about save compatibility.
claims.locator: 'Code freeze and system versioning': 'This can only occur up to a certain point, otherwise the s[ystem ...]'; the discussion frames versioning as the mechanism that bounds change
claims.context: Brooks (1975) via secondary summary; the passage is about system versioning generally, applied here as an analogy for save-schema versioning.

claims.statement: No published rate of save-incompatibility incidents across patches was located; the missing measurement is the share of patches that invalidate existing saves for a sample of live titles.
claims.locator: the source documents the mechanism but gives no incident rate
claims.context: Gap statement.

claims.statement: Crunch is common rather than exceptional: across all IGDA DSS 2023 respondents, '28% said their job involved crunch time and a further 25% said that their job required periods of long hours, extended work hours, or extended overtime, that they just didn't call crunch'.
claims.locator: 'Snapshot: Hours of Work': 'Across all respondents, 28% said their job involved crunch time and a further 25% said that their job required periods of long hours ... that they just didn't call crunch.'
claims.context: IGDA/Western University DSS 2023, self-reported, voluntary sample. The 28% + 25% = 53% combined incidence is the actionable figure, since the second group is uncounted by most reporting.

claims.statement: The detection signal is repeat incidence, not first occurrence: 'among those who experienced crunch, 63% of employees, 64% of freelancers, and 75% of the self-employed had crunched more than twice in the past two years'.
claims.locator: 'Among those who experienced crunch, 63% of employees, 64% of freelancers, and 75% of the self-employed had crunched more than twice in the past two years (Figure 11). This is notably higher than the 2021 DSS where about 58% of employees, 64% of freelancers, and 63% of the self-employed engaged in crunch at that rate.'
claims.context: IGDA DSS 2023 vs 2021. The 2021 comparison shows the employee rate rose from about 58% to 63%.

claims.statement: Crunch is a schedule risk as well as a welfare risk: a third of respondents received no additional compensation for overtime or crunch and only 13% received paid overtime or a lump sum, so unpaid crunch is not self-correcting through compensation - it converts directly into attrition risk.
claims.locator: 'Overtime remains poorly compensated (Figure 21). One-third received no additional compensation for working beyond normal office hours (i.e., overtime or crunch). Only 13% received paid overtime or a lump sum payment and 7% received a combination of money and compensatory time. Almost one-quarter (23%) received time off in exchange for overtime worked.'
claims.context: IGDA DSS 2023. 'One-third' is the source's own rounding; the exact percentage is not stated.

claims.statement: The quantitative mitigation case is Brooks' productivity spread and the quadratic coordination cost: 'good programmers are generally five to ten times as productive as mediocre ones', while communication channels grow as n(n-1)/2, so buying capacity with hours or headcount has sharply diminishing returns.
claims.locator: 'The surgical team': 'good programmers are generally five to ten times as productive as mediocre ones'; 'Communication': 1,225 channels of communication for 50 people (n(n-1)/2)
claims.context: Brooks' 5-10x figure is a 1975 estimate from a specific organisation, via a secondary summary; it is widely repeated and widely disputed as a hiring justification. Presented here only as the source's own claim.

game_examples.fact: No game example is offered for crunch/burnout: the evidence here is survey-based (IGDA DSS 2023), because a named studio's crunch is rarely confirmed by a primary, citable source.
game_examples.locator: evidence is SRC-DER-031 (IGDA/Western University DSS 2023), not a game postmortem
game_examples.non_transferable: Do not substitute an unverified industry anecdote for the survey data; the survey's sampling limits must be carried with any use of its numbers.
